Wing Ban in Monaco
After the high rear wings on both Lotus 49b had
broken at highspeed at the previous Grand Prix
in Spain - leading to serious accidents involving
Graham Hill and Jochen Rindt - there had already
been a row between Rindt and Lotus boss Colin
Chapman ahead of the Monaco Grand Prix. In a
letter, the Austrian accused Chapman of not taking
the safety of his cars seriously.
The stubborn Briton promptly replaced the Austrian
with Richard Attwood for Monaco. But the Monaco
organisers themselves also had serious concerns
that, should a similar accident occur on the narrow
street circuit in the Principality, spectators could
lose their lives.
It was agreed that the wings would initially be
permitted in practice but banned for the race.
The rear wing was not allowed to be higher than
the highest point of the car. For the teams, this
meant a considerable amount of modification
work, but the two race directors, Paul Frére and
Charles Deutsch, were unwilling to take any risks.
Jo Siffert’s privately entered Lotus 49b also presen-
ted an unusual sight after these modifications. The
Swiss driver made the most of his talent despite
the inferior car and managed to secure a place on
the podium in third - just ahead of Team Lotus’s
stand-in driver Attwood. From the following Dutch
Grand Prix onwards, all cars were fitted with new,
flat but large rear wings.
Lotus 49B Cosworth V8 F1 Rob Walker 3° Monaco GP 1969

Too late to succeed
Following its major rally successes with the Escort,
Ford was urgently seeking a successor for the
World Rally Championship from 1983. However,
the Group B competition from Lancia, Audi and
Peugeot had by then set the bar very high, and the
advent of four-wheel drive technology now requi-
red a significantly greater investment.
None other than former Formula 1 designer Tony
Southgate designed a prototype featuring what
was perhaps the finest Group B rally chassis ever.
However, the RS200 turned out to be a little too
heavy and, with its 450 hp, was also outclassed by
the competition in terms of power. To make mat-
ters worse, WRC homologation was delayed until
February 1986.
As a result, the new mid-engined Ford missed its
eagerly awaited debut at the Monte Carlo Rally. It
was not until the 1986 Swedish Rally that Kalle
Grundel and Benny Melander took to the start line
for the first time in the new works car, setting three
fastest special stage times in the snow of their
home rally and engaging in a close battle with Juha
Kankkunen’s Peugeot and Markku Alén’s Lancia.
Third place on its debut was promising, but it re-
mained the RS200’s best result in the World
Championship, as the end of the brutal Group B
cars was drawing near following Henri Toivonen’s
fatal accident. The 600 hp evolution car planned
for 1987 was never fielded in the WRC.
Ford RS200 Ford Motor Co. Ltd. 3° Rallye Sweden 1986
